ann_42.text: This part acts on 68 of 242 training patients (28%); 38 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 65-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 1 vessel coloured, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a normal thallium scan), it slightly lowers the predicted risk, from about 98% to about 94% (on the training data only).

Through it, older age lowers a typical patient's predicted risk, with nothing until about 60 years, then steadily: from about 26% at 42 years to about 8% at 66 years, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower (on the training data only).

ann_43.text: Through this part, higher resting blood pressure lowers a typical patient's predicted risk, with nothing until about 112 mm Hg, then steadily: from about 54% at 110 mm Hg to about 6% at 155 mm Hg, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower (on the training data only).
It does so only once resting blood pressure rises above about 131 mm Hg (for the typical patient with a fold, from about 54% to about 4%; on the training data only).
An ST segment that is not upsloping raises the predicted risk here from about 26% to about 54% (on the training data only).

In the model as a whole, higher resting blood pressure clearly raises the predicted risk, quickly at first, then levels off, and even more so if the ST segment is not upsloping (from about 37% to about 75%, against about 22% to about 29% with an upsloping one).

ann_44.text: This part acts on the 42 of 242 training patients (17%) with atypical angina; 8 of them had heart disease.
For the typical patient it acts on (a 52-year-old man with atypical angina and a normal thallium scan), it lowers the predicted risk from about 15% to about 7% (on the training data only).
Through it, atypical angina lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 12% (on the training data only).

ann_45.text: This part acts on 59 of 242 training patients (24%); 19 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 55-year-old woman with atypical angina, an upsloping ST segment and a normal thallium scan), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from below 1% to about 2% (on the training data only).
Through it, atypical angina raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 37% (on the training data only).

Each extra vessel coloured adds about the same, and both more vessels and a downsloping ST segment raise the predicted risk more with atypical angina (from 0 to 2 vessels, about 7% to about 75% against about 26% to about 84% with other chest pain types; a downsloping ST segment, about 7% to about 57% against about 26% to about 54%). The model has little data on this: only 17 training patients have a downsloping ST segment.
Being a woman clearly lowers it, and even more so without atypical angina (from about 26% to about 3%, against about 7% to about 1%).
For the typical patient it acts on, a downsloping ST segment raises it from about 2% to about 9% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this, 17 patients).

ann_46.text: This part acts on 142 of 242 training patients (59%); 82 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 1.4 mm of ST depression, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it raises the predicted risk from about 89% to about 95% (on the training data only).

Through it, more ST depression on exercise raises a typical patient's predicted risk slowly at first, then faster, once it rises above about 0.4 mm: from about 20% at 0 mm to about 70% at 2.8 mm (on the training data only).

ann_47.text: This part acts on 199 of 242 training patients (82%); 75 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 57-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 0.3 mm of ST depression, an upsloping ST segment and a normal thallium scan), it raises the predicted risk from about 4% to about 32% (on the training data only).

Through it, more ST depression on exercise lowers a typical patient's predicted risk in an uneven way, from about 46% at 0 mm to about 5% at 2.8 mm, and a flat ST segment lowers it from about 26% to about 5% (on the training data only).

Older age raises it here in an uneven way, from about 12% at 42 to about 41% at 66 years; typical angina raises it to about 39%; and a higher maximum heart rate also raises it in an uneven way, from about 21% at 118 to about 30% at 175 beats per minute (on the training data only).

Age clearly matters more here if the ST segment is not flat and if ST depression is 0.8 mm or less, in both cases with the predicted risk highest at about 60 years and lower either side: a typical patient goes from about 7% at 42 to about 21% at 66 years without a flat ST segment (against about 57% to about 60% with one), and from about 12% to about 31% with ST depression of 0.8 mm or less (against about 8% to about 18%).

In the model as a whole, more ST depression clearly raises the predicted risk in an uneven way, and even more so with a flat ST segment (from about 75% to about 94%, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher, against about 38% to about 27% otherwise).

ann_48.text: Through this part, each extra vessel coloured adds about the same: going from 0 to 2 vessels raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 84% (on the training data only).
A reversible thallium defect raises it to about 51% (on the training data only).
Higher cholesterol raises it steadily, from about 17% at 193 mg/dL to about 44% at 308 mg/dL (on the training data only).
Being a woman lowers it to about 3%, and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 12% (on the training data only).
For two rare thallium results the model has little data on this: a result coded 4 (2 patients; about 79%) and a fixed defect (15 patients; about 15%), both on the training data only.
An abnormal resting ECG raises it only slightly here, from about 26% to about 30% (on the training data only).

ann_49.text: Through it, age changes a typical patient's predicted risk only slightly, highest at about 60 years and lower either side, with about 17% at 42 years and about 12% at 66 years (on the training data only).

ann_50.text: Through this part, an ST segment that is not upsloping raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 54% (on the training data only).
Higher resting blood pressure raises it quickly at first, then levels off: from about 22% at 110 mm Hg to about 29% at 155 mm Hg (on the training data only).

ann_51.text: Through this part, typical angina (about 4%) and non-anginal chest pain (about 7%) clearly lower a typical patient's predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms (about 26%).
Being a woman clearly lowers it, and even more so without chest pain symptoms (from about 26% to about 3%, against about 7% to about 1% with atypical angina).
Each extra vessel coloured clearly adds about the same, and even more so with atypical angina (from 0 to 2 vessels, about 7% to about 75%, against about 26% to about 84% without chest pain symptoms).

A downsloping ST segment raises it, and even more so with atypical angina (from about 7% to about 57%, against about 26% to about 54%). The model has little data on this: only 17 training patients (a downsloping ST segment).

A thallium result coded 4 raises it, and even more so without chest pain symptoms (from about 26% to about 79%, against about 7% to about 31% with atypical angina). The model has little data on this: only 2 training patients (thallium stress test result coded 4 (meaning not recorded)).
Only 2 training patients have a thallium result coded 4.

ann_52.text: Through this part, older age raises a typical patient's predicted risk in an uneven way, from about 12% at 42 to about 41% at 66 years; a flat ST segment raises it to about 42%, typical angina to about 39%, and chest pain brought on by exercise to about 38% (on the training data only).
A higher maximum heart rate lowers it here in an uneven way, from about 31% at 118 to about 23% at 175 beats per minute (on the training data only).

Age adds to the predicted risk through this part with nothing until about 58 years (between 36 and 58 years for different patients), then steadily, and only slightly (for the typical patient with a fold, from about 95% to about 97%, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher); this holds for most patients, but for patients without chest pain on exercise and patients with an upsloping ST segment it rises steadily (on the training data only).

ann_53.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina or non-anginal chest pain (about 7% each) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 26%).

More vessels coloured and higher cholesterol both raise a typical patient's predicted risk steadily, from about 26% at 0 vessels to about 84% at 2, and from about 17% at 193 mg/dL to about 44% at 308 mg/dL; a flat ST segment raises it to about 71%, and a reversible thallium defect to about 51% (on the training data only).

Being a woman lowers it to about 3% and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 12%; a higher maximum heart rate lowers it in an uneven way, from about 31% at 118 to about 23% at 175 beats per minute; and higher resting blood pressure raises it quickly at first, then levels off, from about 22% at 110 to about 29% at 155 mm Hg (on the training data only).

By age, the predicted risk is highest at about 60 years and lower either side, from about 7% at 42 years to about 21% at 66 years for a typical patient, and chest pain brought on by exercise raises it to about 38% (on the training data only).

For three rare categories the model has little data on this: a thallium result coded 4 (2 patients; about 79%), a downsloping ST segment (17 patients; about 54%) and a fixed thallium defect (15 patients; about 15%), all on the training data only.
An abnormal resting ECG raises it only slightly, from about 26% to about 30% (on the training data only).

ann_42.original: Hypothesis: 1499 = relu(1.461 age_z - 0.900) is an older-age hinge, zero below age_z 0.616 and linear above (active for 28% of train rows). Its output enters age_effect with weight -1.542, which outweighs the +0.377 direct age slope, so it turns the age effect downward for the oldest ~28%. Evidence (train, n=242): affine fit R2 0.49 (a real kink); mean-ablating it drops train AUC 0.9515 -> 0.9436, linearising it 0.9515 -> 0.9467; logit-contribution SD 0.73.
ann_42.proposed: Age above about 60 years lowers the predicted risk through this part.

ann_43.original: Hypothesis: 3392 = relu(0.823 + 1.448 trestbps_z + 0.769 slope:1_z) is a resting-BP hinge whose threshold depends on upsloping ST: on for trestbps_z > -0.06 without upslope and > -1.13 with upslope (68% active). 5768 = 0.562 + 1.204*3392 never clips on train (min 0.56), so it only relays 3392. In bp_effect it is subtracted (-0.686), cancelling most of the direct BP slope above the hinge. Evidence: 3392 affine R2 0.90; mean-ablation AUC 0.9515 -> 0.9292 (the largest single-unit drop); linearising 3392 gives 0.9486; tool sensitivity d5768/d(trestbps, slope:1) = 1.18, 0.63.
ann_43.proposed: Resting blood pressure above about 131 mm Hg lowers the predicted risk through this part; an ST segment that is not upsloping raises it.

ann_44.original: Hypothesis: 2350 = relu(0.732 cp:2_z + 0.156) is an exact indicator of atypical angina (cp:2): 0 for other chest-pain types, 1.753 for cp:2 (17% of rows). Weighted -0.531 it lowers the logit by 0.93 for cp:2 patients. Evidence: affine R2 1.0 on the binary data domain (linearising leaves AUC at 0.9515); mean-ablation AUC 0.9475.
ann_44.proposed: An indicator of atypical angina that lowers the predicted risk.

ann_45.original: Hypothesis: 3683 = relu(-0.956 + 1.114 cp:2 - 0.529 sex:1 + 0.582 ca + 0.542 slope:3 - 0.715 thal:4) adds risk (+0.824 weight) for atypical-angina patients in proportion to being female, having more fluoroscopy-coloured vessels (ca) and downsloping ST. It is on for 100% of cp:2 patients, 22% of non-cp:2 women (those with high ca or slope:3) and 1.5% of non-cp:2 men. With cp2_indicator it makes the cp:2 effect sex-dependent: chest_pain_effect mean +0.42 for cp:2 women vs -0.52 for cp:2 men. Evidence: affine R2 0.74; mean-ablation AUC 0.9445, linearised 0.9479; tool sensitivities (cp:2, sex:1, ca, slope:3, thal:4) = 0.27, 0.13, 0.14, 0.13, 0.17. thal:4 has n=2 in train, so its term is essentially unsupported.
ann_45.proposed: A part acting on 59 patients: atypical angina raises the predicted risk through it, and with atypical angina more vessels and a downsloping ST segment raise it more.

ann_46.original: Hypothesis: 4072 = relu(1.046 oldpeak_z + 0.570) is zero for no or minimal exercise ST depression (oldpeak_z < -0.545; 41% of rows, which includes every oldpeak=0 row) and linear above; weighted +1.044 it adds ~1.09 logit per SD of ST depression. Evidence: affine R2 0.985 over the data (most of the effect is linear; linearised AUC 0.9508) but mean-ablating it drops AUC to 0.9369; logit-contribution SD 0.98.
ann_46.proposed: ST depression above about 0.4 mm raises the predicted risk.

ann_47.original: Hypothesis: 245 = relu(0.845 + 0.237 thalach + 0.202 cp:1 - 1.638 oldpeak - 1.293 slope:2 + 0.121 relu(0.995 thalach - 1.590)) scores a NORMAL exercise response: active for 100% of oldpeak=0 rows and 92% of non-flat-slope rows, but only 29% of flat-slope (slope:2) rows and 10% of rows with oldpeak_z > 0.5 (corr with disease -0.46). 5302 (high-thalach hinge) is on for 3.7% of rows and is inert (mean-ablation AUC unchanged at 0.9515). 5402 = 0.354 + 1.107*245 never clips, so 4376 = relu(-0.857 + 2.129 age + 2.396*245): an age x normal-ST interaction, large for older patients with a normal ST response and zero for young patients with abnormal ST. Both exits ADD logit (0.167*245 + 0.282*4376; mean +1.19, SD 1.14, range 0..4.19) even though they correlate negatively with disease (-0.36): the module offsets the large positive slope:2/oldpeak terms elsewhere in exercise_test_effect and carries a positive age slope for patients with normal ST (see exercise_test_effect). Evidence: mean-ablating the module drops AUC 0.9515 -> 0.9334 (245 alone 0.9356, 4376 alone 0.9377); tool sensitivity of 4376 to (cp:1, thalach, oldpeak, slope:2, age) = 0.27, 0.32, 2.17, 1.72, 1.59.
ann_47.proposed: A part that acts on most patients and raises their predicted risk: through it ST depression and a flat ST segment lower the risk, and older age raises it more when the ST segment is not flat.

ann_48.original: Hypothesis: identity_linear is the purely linear part of the logit over eight inputs: 1.189 ca + 1.161 sex:1 + 0.568 chol + 0.327 fbs:0 - 0.087 restecg:0 - 0.525 thal:3 + 0.117 thal:4 - 0.427 thal:6 (z-scored). More vessels, male sex, higher cholesterol and normal fasting sugar raise risk; normal thallium (thal:3) and fixed defect (thal:6) lower it. Evidence: range -4.55..5.63, SD 2.05; alone it gives train AUC 0.844; mean-ablating it drops the model to 0.8774 (largest component). SHAP (prob. scale, full train): ca 0.126, sex:1 0.106, thal:3 0.061, chol 0.045.
ann_48.proposed: An additive part: more vessels, a reversible thallium defect and higher cholesterol raise the predicted risk; being a woman and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL lower it.

ann_49.original: Hypothesis: identity_age = 0.377 age_z - 1.542 age_hinge(age_z) is an inverted-V age shape: rising slowly to a peak at age_z 0.616 then falling steeply (slope -1.87 per SD above it). Component curve at age_z -1.96/-0.75/0.13/0.76/1.23/1.69 = -0.74/-0.28/0.05/-0.04/-0.92/-1.78. Age also enters through normal_st_age_module (4376), so the full-model partial dependence on age is a softer inverted U: -1.20/-0.41/0.21/0.44/-0.16/-0.75 at the same ages. Evidence: logit SD 0.54; mean-ablating the component drops AUC to 0.9466.
ann_49.proposed: Through this part, older age slightly lowers the predicted risk.

ann_50.original: Hypothesis: identity_bp = 1.296 trestbps_z - 0.686*(0.562 + 1.204 relu(0.823 + 1.448 trestbps_z + 0.769 slope:1_z)) = -0.385 + 1.296 trestbps - 0.826 relu(...): resting BP raises risk with slope 1.30/SD below the hinge and only 0.10/SD above it (saturating). The hinge sits at trestbps_z -0.06 without upsloping ST and -1.13 with it, so with upsloping ST almost the whole BP range is in the flat regime and the logit is lowered by up to 1.27 at a given BP (fully, once BP is above the no-upslope hinge). summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results, predicted risk of heart disease about 26%), the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk with typical angina or non-anginal chest pain (about 7% each).

More vessels coloured by fluoroscopy and higher cholesterol both raise the predicted risk steadily: for a typical patient, going from 0 to 2 vessels raises it from about 26% to about 84%, and cholesterol from 193 to 308 mg/dL from about 17% to about 44%; a flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises it to about 71%, and a reversible defect on the thallium scan to about 51% (on the training data only).
Being a woman lowers it to about 3%, and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 12% (on the training data only).

More ST depression on exercise clearly raises the predicted risk in an uneven way, and even more so if the ST segment is flat: going from 0 to 2.8 mm moves it from about 75% to about 94% with a flat ST segment, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher, against about 38% to about 27% otherwise.

By age, the predicted risk is highest at about 60 years and lower either side (for a typical patient about 7% at 42 years and about 21% at 66 years), and chest pain brought on by exercise raises it to about 38% (on the training data only).
For two rare thallium results the model has little data on this: a result coded 4 (2 patients; about 79%) and a fixed defect (15 patients; about 15%), both on the training data only.
